title: When to fine tune, and the three cheaper things to try first
story:
When a system is almost right, the instinct is to train it on your own data. It sounds like the serious answer, the one that demonstrates commitment, and it is usually both the most expensive response available and a response to the wrong problem. So before the decision, get precise about what fine-tuning actually changes.

Three cheaper things come first, in this order.

Write a clearer instruction. Most disappointing output is a faithful response to an ambiguous request, and the ambiguity is invisible to whoever wrote it. State the task as if for a competent stranger, state the shape of the output, and state what to produce when the task cannot be done. A surprising share of the problems that prompt a fine-tuning proposal disappear here, which is embarrassing only if you skip it.

Put examples in the input. Demonstrations carry what definitions cannot, particularly for tone, formatting and the treatment of awkward cases. This costs window space on every request and nothing else, and it tells you quickly whether the behaviour you want is available at all from this model.

Supply the facts through retrieval. If the failure is that the system does not know something, that is not a training problem, and the evidence is fairly direct. Ovadia and colleagues compared unsupervised fine-tuning with retrieval on knowledge-intensive tasks and found that retrieval consistently outperforms it, both for knowledge the model met in pre-training and for new information — and that models struggle to learn new factual information through unsupervised fine-tuning at all, with the suggestion that many variations of the same fact might be needed to help.

Take the general rule from that, because it is the sentence worth carrying out of this lesson: fine-tuning teaches form, retrieval supplies facts. If your complaint begins with it does not know, you are looking at a retrieval problem wearing a training problem's clothes, and training will cost you a month and leave the gap where it was.

Which leaves the cases where fine-tuning is genuinely the right tool, and they are real. A consistent form you can demonstrate but cannot describe — a house style, a specific structure, a particular way of handling edge cases — where examples in the window would be too many to afford on every request. A narrow task with plenty of labelled data, where you want a small model to do a large model's job at a fraction of the cost and latency. A behaviour that is easy to show and hard to specify, which is the same argument as learning from comparisons, one level down.

The economics changed too, and it is worth knowing so that the objection is accurate. Hu, Shen and colleagues introduced a method that freezes the pre-trained weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer, reducing the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times against fine-tuning a model of 175 billion parameters with a standard optimiser, cutting accelerator memory by 3 times, performing on par with or better than full fine-tuning in quality, and — unlike adapter layers — adding no additional inference latency. So this is not too expensive to attempt; that objection is mostly out of date.

What remains expensive is everything around it. The labelled dataset, which is people's time and the place where the quality actually comes from. The evaluation you need in order to know whether it worked, which you should have built before you started. And the permanent fact that you now own a model: a version to track, an artefact to store, a thing to re-train when the base moves underneath it, and one more component that can change behaviour without anyone changing code. The training run is the cheap part, and it is the part everyone estimates.

problem.name: Choosing between instruction, evidence and training
problem.shape: The system is close to right, and several remedies of wildly different cost would all plausibly help.
tell: the complaint starts with the words it does not know
no one has yet tried stating the task for a stranger who cannot ask questions
examples have never been put in the input
the case set that would show whether training helped does not exist yet
problem.move: Try a clearer instruction, then examples in the input, then retrieval. Fine-tune only when the gap is in form rather than in facts, or when a small model must do a narrow job cheaply — and build the evaluation before the dataset.
problem.invariant: Fine-tuning teaches form and retrieval supplies facts, so a failure that begins with the system not knowing something is a retrieval problem however it is phrased.
problem.breaks: Models struggle to learn new factual information through unsupervised fine-tuning, so training as a way to inject knowledge underperforms retrieval both for new information and for what the model already met.

cost.time: the labelled dataset and the evaluation are the real work, while the training run is the part everyone estimates
cost.space: you now own a versioned artefact to store, track and re-train when the base model moves
cost.beats: prompting and retrieval, which are cheaper and cannot impose a consistent form at scale, and a larger model, which costs more on every request forever

worked.reasoning:
It is for form, not for facts. That one distinction settles most of these arguments.

Before reaching for it I try three cheaper things in order. A clearer instruction, written for a competent stranger who cannot ask questions, with the output shape and the failure output stated — a surprising share of fine-tuning proposals dissolve here. Then examples in the input, which carry tone, formatting and the treatment of awkward cases in a way definitions cannot, and which cost only window space. Then retrieval, if the failure is that the system does not know something.

The evidence for that last one is direct. Ovadia and colleagues compared unsupervised fine-tuning with retrieval on knowledge-intensive tasks and found retrieval consistently outperforms it, for information met in pre-training and for new information, and that models struggle to learn new factual information through unsupervised fine-tuning at all. So a complaint that starts with it does not know is a retrieval problem wearing a training problem's clothes.

Where fine-tuning genuinely wins: a consistent form I can demonstrate but not describe, where carrying enough examples in the window on every request is unaffordable; a narrow task with plenty of labelled data, where a small model should do a large model's job at lower cost and latency; and behaviour easy to show and hard to specify.

On cost, I would be accurate rather than dismissive. Hu, Shen and colleagues freeze the pre-trained weights and inject trainable rank decomposition matrices per layer, reducing trainable parameters by 10,000 times against fine-tuning a 175 billion parameter model with a standard optimiser, cutting accelerator memory by 3 times, matching or beating full fine-tuning in quality, and adding no additional inference latency unlike adapters. So too expensive to attempt is out of date.

What stays expensive is the labelled dataset, the evaluation I need to know it worked, and owning a versioned artefact that must be re-trained when the base moves. The training run is the cheap part and the part everyone estimates.

problem.practice: Write down the failure you want fine-tuning to fix, in one sentence, then classify it: is it about form or about facts? If any part of the sentence is about the system not knowing something, split that part off and send it to retrieval before you go anywhere near a dataset.

beats.broke: An almost-right system invites training on your own data, which is the costliest remedy and often aimed at a gap training cannot close.
beats.fix: Instruction, then examples in the input, then retrieval — and fine-tune only for form, for a narrow task with labels, or to make a small model do a large one's job.
beats.cost: The dataset, the evaluation and owning a versioned artefact are the real costs, while the training run is the part that gets estimated.

interview.q: What is fine-tuning for, what is it not for, and what would you try first?
interview.trap: Reaching for training to add knowledge. Retrieval consistently outperforms unsupervised fine-tuning for knowledge injection, and models struggle to learn new facts that way at all.

Fine-tuning genuinely wins for a consistent form I can demonstrate but not describe and cannot afford to carry as examples on every request; for a narrow task with plenty of labels where a small model should do a large model's job cheaply; and for behaviour easy to show and hard to specify.

On cost I would be accurate: freezing the weights and injecting trainable rank decomposition matrices per layer cuts trainable parameters by 10,000 times against fine-tuning a 175 billion parameter model with a standard optimiser, cuts accelerator memory by 3 times, matches or beats full fine-tuning in quality and adds no inference latency, unlike adapters — so the expense objection is out of date.
